tip: Remembering happens to you in Korean – 생각나요 (saenggangnayo) means the memory 'comes up' by itself. The old teacher surfaces in your mind; you're not the one doing the thinking.
생일 축하해요 (saengil chukhahaeyo) is literally 'I congratulate your birthday' – 축하하다 (chukhahada) is a verb, so Korean congratulates the day rather than wishing it happy.
환갑 (hwangap) marks 예순 살 (yesun sal), the 60th birthday – one full cycle of the traditional 60-year calendar, which is why it gets its own name and a big family celebration.
-마다 (-mada) glues 'every' straight onto a noun: 생일마다 (saengil-mada) = every birthday. No separate word needed – the noun itself carries it.
Korean won't state someone else's feelings directly – 온 가족이 기뻐해요 (on gajogi gippeohaeyo) uses -어하다 (-eohada), 'shows happiness'. Plain 기뻐요 (gippeoyo) is only for your own joy.
긴장돼요 (ginjangdwaeyo) is built on 되다 (doeda), 'become' – nerves happen to you in Korean, not something you are. 되 (doe) + 어 (eo) fuses into the 돼 (dwae) you see here.
답답해요 (dapdaphaeyo) covers stuffy rooms and stuck conversations alike – talk that's 안 통해서 (an tonghaeseo), not flowing through, feels literally airless in Korean.
A noun can't guess on its own – it needs the linking 인 (in): 사람인 것 같아요 (saramin geot gatayo) = 'seems to be a (good) person'. Verbs and adjectives skip that link.
Korean negates inside the guess: 아닌 것 같아요 (anin geot gatayo) is 'seems to not be true', where English pulls the no forward into 'I don't think it's true'.
The -죠 (-jyo) ending turns a statement into a nudge for agreement – 그렇죠 (geureochyo) is 'that's so, right?'. Drop it and you're just stating a fact.
할게요 (halgeyo) is not a plain future – the -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) ending promises the listener: 'I'll do it, count on it'. A neutral guess would use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (-l geoyeyo) instead.
그렇군요 (geureokunyo) carries the -군요 (-gunyo) ending, which flags information you just took in – an out-loud 'oh, I see'. Without it, 그래요 (geuraeyo) is flat agreement.
글쎄요 (geulsseyo) buys time politely – and it's often a soft no in disguise. When a Korean answer starts with 글쎄요, don't count on a yes.
아마 (ama), 'probably', can't sit on a flat statement – it wants a guessing ending to match: 아마 그럴 거예요 (ama geureol geoyeyo). The word and the ending agree on uncertainty.
-지 않아요 (-ji anayo) is the long-form 'not': 생각하지 않아요 (saenggakhaji anayo) = I don't think so. More measured than fronting 안 (an) – handy for polite disagreement.
One-word reactions still carry politeness: 요 (yo) tacked onto 정말 (jeongmal) gives 정말요? (jeongmallyo) – a polite 'really?'. The bare word alone is for close friends.
보다 (boda) marks the standard of comparison and attaches to it: 버스보다 (beoseu-boda) = than the bus. KTX가 (KTX-ga) carries only the subject marker – no 'than' word on it.
건강에 좋아요 (geongang-e joayo) = good for your health – the particle 에 (e) points at what something is good (or bad) for. No 'for' word; the particle does it.
딱딱해요 (ttakttakhaeyo), 'hard', doubles its syllable to mimic the feel – Korean texture words often work this way: the sound itself imitates the sensation.
훨씬 커요 (hwolssin keoyo) = far bigger, not just bigger – 훨씬 turns a comparison up to 'by far'. Plain 더 (deo) is a mere 'more'.
생각보다 (saenggak-boda) is literally 'than thought' – a ready-made 'than I expected'. Korean compares straight against the noun for your expectation, no verb needed.
Preferences reuse the comparison particle: 여름보다 겨울을 좋아해요 (yeoreum-boda gyeoureul joahaeyo) = like winter more than summer. No word for 'more' – 보다 (boda) implies it.
덜 (deol) is the mirror of 더 (deo): 덜 추워요 (deol chuwoyo) = less cold. English rebuilds the sentence with 'not as cold as'; Korean just swaps in 덜.
제일 (jeil) in front of an adjective makes the superlative: 제일 맛있어요 (jeil masisseoyo) = the tastiest. Nothing about the adjective changes – the little word does all the work.
중에서 (jung-eseo) scopes a superlative to a group: 가족 중에서 (gajok jung-eseo) = among the family. Without it, 제일 커요 (jeil keoyo) would mean tallest of everyone.
가장 (gajang) and 제일 (jeil) both mean 'most', but 가장 leans slightly formal and written – 가장 좋아요 (gajang joayo) sounds a touch more composed than 제일 좋아요 (jeil joayo).
Popularity is something you have in Korean: 인기가 많아요 (ingi-ga manayo) is literally 'popularity is much'. Friends work the same way – 친구가 많아요 (chingu-ga manayo).
월급날 (wolgeumnal) hides a sound shift: the ㅂ (b) of 월급 (wolgeup) turns into ㅁ (m) before the ㄴ (n) of 날 (nal). Korean smooths consonant clashes like this constantly.
처럼 (cheoreom) means 'like' and glues straight onto the noun: 가수처럼 (gasu-cheoreom) = like a singer. No separate 'as' or 'like' floating in the sentence – the particle carries it.
주말마다 (jumal-mada) = every weekend – 마다 (mada) already carries the 'each and every', so the noun never pluralizes: no 'weekends' needed.
마음이 바다처럼 넓어요 (maeum-i bada-cheoreom neolbeoyo) – a generous heart is 'wide' in Korean, not big. Wide as the sea is the stock image for a forgiving nature.
Respect extends to a person's traits: 부드러우세요 (budeureouseyo) takes the honorific -(으)세요 (-(eu)seyo) because the voice belongs to the 팀장님 (timjangnim). Even their qualities get honored.
English loans turn into verbs with 하다 (hada): 체크인하고 싶어요 (chekeuinhago sipeoyo) is literally 'want to do check-in'. The same trick gives 쇼핑하다 (syopinghada) = to shop.
부탁해요 (butakhaeyo) literally asks a favor: 'I entrust this to you'. It turns a bare noun like 방 (bang), room, into a full polite request – no command verb needed.
조식 (josik) is hotel-register breakfast – the formal word you'll meet at check-in and on signs. In everyday talk, breakfast is just 아침 (achim), 'morning'.
펜션 (pensyeon) is a false friend – in Korea it's a rental holiday guesthouse, a family-trip staple, not a retirement pension. Unlike a hotel room, it usually comes with a kitchen.
Korean likes to pivot with a fresh sentence: 예약했어요 (yeyakhaesseoyo). 그런데 (geureonde)... – 'but' starts sentence two instead of folding into the middle of sentence one.
안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) stretches 되다 (doeda), 'become', into 'it doesn't work' – heaters, plans, phones, anything failing to function. One phrase covers most complaints.
잘못 (jalmot) in front of a verb means you did it wrong: 잘못 봤어요 (jalmot bwasseoyo) = 'saw it wrongly', i.e. misread. It works with almost any verb – hear, press, send.
쯤 (jjeum) suffixes straight onto the amount: 세 시간쯤 (se sigan-jjeum) = about three hours. No separate 'about' word – the approximation rides on the number itself.
편도표보다 (pyeondopyo-boda), 'than a one-way ticket', can lead the whole sentence – 보다 (boda) marks the comparison wherever it sits, so the word order stays flexible.
가르치다 (gareuchida) isn't just classroom teaching – 길을 가르쳐 줬어요 (gireul gareuchyeo jwosseoyo) means she 'taught the road', i.e. showed the way. Directions are taught in Korean.
Korean narrates forgetting as two actions: 놓고 왔어요 (noko wasseoyo) = 'put it down and came'. There's no single 'leave behind' verb – the sequence of events is the expression.
Memories arise on their own in Korean – 생겼어요 (saenggyeosseoyo), from 생기다 (saenggida), means they 'came into being'. You don't make 추억 (chueok), memories; they happen to you.
Korean counts days with native words of their own: 이틀 (iteul) = two days, 하루 (haru) = one day – not number + 'day'. So 이틀 더 (iteul deo) = two more days, no counter needed.
